title: JAGDA Exhibition 2026
description: An audio guide to JAGDA Exhibition 2026 at Tokyo Midtown Design Hub (Oct 2–25, 11:00–19:00, free). Five designers from each of eight regions of Japan, one stop per region. Indoors, GPS can’t tell the rooms apart: tap each region in the list when you reach it.

intro.title: Welcome to JAGDA Exhibition 2026
intro.text:
Welcome to JAGDA Exhibition 2026, the 121st exhibition at Tokyo Midtown Design Hub.

Graphic design in Japan used to be a big-city story. Today it grows everywhere, rooted in local places. JAGDA, the Japan Graphic Designers Association, has about three thousand members across the country. For this second edition, its committee chose forty designers and teams from eight regions: Hokkaido, Tohoku, Kanto-Koshinetsu, Tokyo, Chubu, Kansai, Chugoku-Shikoku, and Kyushu. Five from each.

The statement is called Design Geothermal: the heat that rises from the ground. It asks a hard question. How do we stay human, and stay close to our places, in a world of super-intelligent AI that can leave people behind? Its answer: love is close to heat. Use that heat, and cross borders.

Each region also made its own poster for the show. You will find them with the work.

Tap a region when you reach it. Each stop is about a minute.

stops.title: Hokkaido
stops.teaser: Adachi · Sanbongi · Nishimoto · Nomura · Pichik Pachik
stops.text:
Hokkaido. Five designers, most of them based in Sapporo.

Shiori Adachi runs Shiori Graphic. Look for her peeeel works: layers of coloured paper, cut and peeled back, then photographed. They won prizes in Taiwan and Toyama. She is now opening a craft drink and gift shop.

Chiyori Sanbongi, born in 1994, works at KD, and has won typography and Sapporo art director awards.

Miyuu Nishimoto studied linguistics before design. Since 2024 she works alone: design, drawing and handcraft. In her words, an activity of moving the hand and placing lines.

Sou Nomura leads Studio Wonder, and has won the Sapporo ADC grand prix.

And Pichik Kato plus Pachik Sakamoto, a duo born in 1995. They make graphics and their own products, and they host the Sapporo ADC parties.

stops.title: Tohoku
stops.text:
Tohoku, the north-east.

Masayuki Kimura, in Aomori, works side by side with local businesses, and helps renovate empty houses. Last year, he says, he bought a whole big storehouse.

Ryohei Yamauchi of grams design office in Iwate wants to send good things out into the world, thinking and worrying with each client.

Yukihiro Enomoto works from Sendai, in Miyagi.

Katsunobu Yoshida, in Yamagata, calls himself a collector, designer and printer. He gathers materials from ecosystems and workplaces and makes his own pigments, for very special printing. You may know his work from 21_21 DESIGN SIGHT across the garden.

And Ichinosuke Takagi, in Iwaki, Fukushima, once worked as a kamaboko fish-cake craftsman. His design for igoku, a local care project for older people, won a Good Design Gold Award.

stops.title: Kanto-Koshinetsu
stops.text:
Kanto-Koshinetsu: the region around Tokyo, out to Niigata.

Ryotaro Sasame, of TRUNK in Kasama, Ibaraki, talks to business owners to find the core they cannot yet put into words. His idea is to raise the purity.

Fumiko Okazeri, of fodesign in Saitama, has won twelve international awards in seven countries.

Ai Akiyoshi came home to Chiba in 2019. Her mission: turn hidden local value into pride.

Naotoshi Kozaki, of KOZAKIKAKU in Kanagawa, uses creativity to make businesses work better, from strategy to logo to film.

And Masashi Tsunoda, in Niigata, looks for the value hidden at the back of things. His work includes a logo for the factory windows of Tsubame-Sanjo, the metalworking towns.

stops.title: Tokyo
stops.text:
Tokyo.

Takuto Okamoto, born in 1998, works across graphics, film, photography, writing and music, looking for new ways of making that push against old frames.

Chiharu Kodama founded ium, and designs everything from brand ideas to identity, web and interfaces.

Takumi Saito, from Niigata, works between Tokyo and Niigata.

Mai Shibatani, an art director at zero, moves between advertising, artist artwork and television.

And Jujiro Maki, born in Okayama, is known for small, sharp flyers, covers and stickers for galleries and independent labels. One of his flyers won the JAGDA Award.

stops.title: Chubu
stops.teaser: Futagami · Nakabayashi + Yasumoto · Murotani · Iida · Hirose
stops.text:
Chubu, the middle of Japan.

Harukimi Futagami, born in 2001, runs a gallery in Takaoka, Toyama. He is also the drummer of a rock band.

Nobuaki Nakabayashi and Sumie Yasumoto, of Tone in Kanazawa, run a design office with a shop and a sweets business next door. So they design from the client's side.

Kaori Murotani works with TSUGI in Fukui, a team known for craft and local product development.

Aya Iida, in Shizuoka, worked at Draft before going independent. Her clients include the Kyoto tea house Ippodo, and Wacoal.

And Rena Hirose, in Nagoya, makes posters, logos and packages, and likes to think by hand.

stops.title: Kansai
stops.text:
Kansai.

Takuma Nishiyama, in Kyoto, turned an old machiya townhouse into Good Time Coffee. Running a real shop shapes his branding.

Mayumi Tamaoka works between Osaka and Awaji Island, where she also runs a community and charity events for dogs and cats.

Shinsuke Suzuki, of Bold in Osaka, likes uniqueness, things you cannot quite understand, and charming waste. Good design, he says, comes from good situations. Ideas often come in the shower. Or not.

Takehiro Wada, of Design Hero in Kobe, runs events and works on social projects. He wants to be someone's hero.

And Ryoko Nagaoka, in Nara, designs books and makes artwork. In 2024 she opened an art book shop called BO/OK.

stops.title: Chugoku-Shikoku
stops.text:
Chugoku and Shikoku, the west.

Koichi Onishi, from Matsue, now leads JAGDA in Shimane.

Hideto Sato, in Okayama, calls his approach native, rooted design.

Nami Yabuki moved from Tokyo to Hiroshima and founded coto.toco. She aims for design where a thing is simply itself.

Akira Kuwahara works quietly, deep in the mountains of Yamaguchi, taking a lot of time to think.

And Asuka Sato, in Tokushima, works near temple sixteen of the Shikoku pilgrimage. She aims for design that warms the heart, and loves morning TV dramas and comedians on the radio.

stops.title: Kyushu and Okinawa
stops.text:
Last, Kyushu and Okinawa.

Hiroto Yazawa, born in 1999, works at Dejima Graph in Nagasaki, and has already won a Pentawards bronze and a Toyama poster prize.

Naotatsu Okuda studied in London, and now teaches in Kumamoto. With friends, he supports children in disaster areas, and grows rice without pesticides.

Yu Inoshita, in Oita, has a long list of awards, including Good Design and the package design prize.

Hitoshi Kawakami, from Osaka, moved to Miyazaki in 2006 and works across ads, brands, web and film.

And Toshikatsu Saji, born in Kyoto and trained in California, runs Sazie Graphics in Okinawa: logos, illustration, shops and craft products.

That is all forty. Before you go, look back at the eight regional posters together. Which heat felt closest to you? Thank you for listening.
